Bauhaus: A design style known for clean shapes and lettering, with a focus on making things simple and useful.
Risograph: A printing method that makes copies using layers of ink, often creating bright colors and a handmade look.
non-autoregressive: An AI that produces its answer all at once instead of one piece at a time.
calibration: How well a model’s confidence matches how often its choices are actually right.
System 1: The quick, automatic kind of thinking that makes snap judgments without much effort.
third-party cookie: A small file placed on your browser by a website other than the one you’re visiting, often to track you across websites.
tag manager: A tool for adding and managing bits of code on a website, often to measure visits or show ads.
open-weight: Describes an AI whose learned settings are available for others to download and use.
VAE: Variational Autoencoder: an AI that learns to squeeze information into a simpler form, then use it to create new examples.
model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
data exfiltration: Taking data out of a computer system without permission.
distillation: Training a smaller AI to imitate the answers of a larger one.
Overton window: The range of ideas that people generally consider acceptable to discuss or support.
ALPR: Automatic license plate recognition: technology that reads vehicle license plates from camera images.
progenitor: An early cell that can develop into a more specialized kind of cell.
in vitro: Done in a lab outside a living body, often using cells in a dish.
neural ectoderm: Early tissue in an embryo that develops into the brain and other parts of the nervous system.
orchestrator: A piece of software that coordinates other programs or AI helpers so they can complete a task.
sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
UUID: Universally unique identifier: a label designed to identify one item without being confused with another.
Tetris effect: When something you’ve done for a long time keeps coming to mind or seems to shape what you notice afterward.
RSS: Really Simple Syndication: a way to collect updates from websites in one place.
HBM: High-bandwidth memory: fast memory placed close to a processor so it can get lots of information quickly.
Glass carrier: A flat piece of glass used as a base to hold thin chip layers while they are assembled.
web-seed: A web server that supplies parts of a torrent download over the internet.
magnet link: A link that tells a file-sharing app how to find a shared file, without containing the file itself.
SHA-256: Secure Hash Algorithm 256: a way to turn data into a fixed-length fingerprint that can help check whether it has changed.
mirror: A copy of a website hosted at a different web address.
VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
management services organizations: Companies that handle business tasks for medical practices, such as billing and staffing, while health professionals provide care.
treble damages: A court-ordered payment of three times the amount of the actual loss.
OpenSolaris: A version of Sun’s Solaris operating system that Sun made available for others to use and change.
SPARC: Scalable Processor Architecture: a design for the chips used in some Sun computers.
x86: A family of chip designs used in many personal computers.
linear content: Video that plays in a set order or schedule, rather than letting viewers choose exactly what to watch and when.
reinforcement learning: A way to train an AI by rewarding choices that work and discouraging choices that do not.
jailbreak resistance: How well an AI resists prompts that try to trick it into breaking its rules.
activated parameters: The parts of an AI’s learned settings that are actually used to answer a particular request.
quantizing: Storing an AI’s internal numbers with fewer digits so it uses less memory and can run faster, sometimes with a small drop in quality.
Millennium Prize Problems: Seven famous, difficult math problems announced with a million-dollar prize for solving each one.
Fields Medal: A major international award for mathematicians, usually given to people under 40 for important work.
decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation: a way to adapt an AI for a new task by training a small add-on instead of changing the whole AI.
Brier score: A measure of how accurate probability guesses are, with lower scores meaning better guesses.
futures: Agreements to buy or sell something later at a price set now, often used to manage or bet on price changes.
board of trade: A marketplace where people trade goods or agreements to buy them later.
ADFGVX: A, D, F, G, V, and X: the six letters used in a German World War I code that scrambled messages to hide them.
substitution cipher: A code that hides a message by replacing each letter or symbol with another one.
pairing mode: A device setting that lets another nearby device find it and connect to it.
vibecoded: Made by asking an AI to write code from prompts, with little hands-on programming.
Lua: A small programming language used to add custom behavior to games and other software.
pixelhunting: Carefully searching a game screen for tiny or hard-to-see things you need to click.
LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
cmudict: Carnegie Mellon University Pronouncing Dictionary: a word list that helps computers know how English words are pronounced.
trie: A way to organize words by their shared beginnings so software can find matching words quickly.
thinking tokens: Small pieces of text an AI uses while working out an answer, including pieces it may not show you.
inference regime: The approach used when an AI produces an answer, such as whether it spends extra time working things out.
RTS: Real-Time Strategy: a game where players build forces and make moves continuously rather than taking turns.
Elo: A score that estimates how strong a player is by comparing their wins and losses against other players.
updating priors: Changing what you initially believe after seeing new evidence.
Model Context Protocol: Model Context Protocol: a shared set of rules that lets AI tools connect to outside apps and information.
context bloat: An overload of extra text given to an AI, which can make its answers less focused and take more time or money to produce.
CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
CRT: Cathode-Ray Tube: a bulky screen technology that makes pictures by lighting tiny spots on glass.
dithering: A way to make extra shades or colors by arranging dots of the colors already available.
anti-aliasing: A way to soften jagged edges in an image so lines look smoother.
dot pitch: The distance between neighboring dots on a screen; closer dots generally make a sharper picture.
JPL: Jet Propulsion Laboratory: a NASA center that designs and runs robotic space missions.
biosignatures: Clues, such as certain chemicals, that could suggest life exists or once existed.
Lean: A computer program used to write mathematical proofs and check that their steps are correct.
Navier-Stokes: The equations scientists use to describe how liquids and gases flow.
CAS: Computer Algebra System: software that can simplify and solve math expressions such as x² + 2x.
gamification: Adding game-like rewards or challenges to encourage people to do something.
micropayments: Very small payments, often just a few cents.
allocator: A part of a program that sets aside and later returns space in the computer for information.
double-free: A programming mistake where software tries to give back the same computer space twice, which can cause crashes or security problems.
combinator: A function that combines other functions or values to make a new one.
carbon capture: Collecting carbon dioxide before it reaches the air, or removing it from the air afterward.
particulate matter: Tiny bits of dust, smoke, or other material floating in the air that can harm people's health.
lathe: A machine that spins a piece of material while a cutting tool shapes it.
mill: A machine that cuts or shapes material, often using a spinning tool.
CNC: Computer Numerical Control: using computer instructions to guide a machine as it cuts or shapes material.
continual learning: An AI's ability to keep learning new things over time without losing what it already learned.
mixture of experts: A way to build an AI from specialist parts, sending each question to the parts best suited to answer it.
catastrophic forgetting: When an AI learns new things but loses older skills or knowledge in the process.
PIP: Performance Improvement Plan: a formal plan that spells out what an employee must improve at work and by when.
Peter principle: The idea that people in a workplace may get promoted until they reach a job they are not good at.
abliteration: A way of changing a language model so it is less likely to refuse requests, by removing patterns linked to refusals.
CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
KL divergence: Kullback–Leibler divergence: a measure of how much one set of possible-outcome chances differs from another, depending on which set is the reference.
Creative Commons: A set of licenses that let creators say how other people may share, reuse, or adapt their work.
decompilation: Turning a program from the form a computer runs into code people can inspect, though the result may not match what its author wrote.
Screen Time: An Apple feature that shows how long someone uses apps and lets them set limits.
Little Snitch: A Mac app that shows when programs try to connect to the internet and lets you block them.
ctid: A PostgreSQL value that points to where a row is stored inside a table, and can change when the row is rewritten.
postings list: A list kept by a search system showing which documents contain a particular word, sometimes with where it appears.
BM25: Best Matching 25: a common search formula that ranks pages by how well their words match a query, while accounting for page length.
left-pad: A small code package that adds chosen characters to the start of text until it reaches a desired length.
mock: A fake version of part of a program, used to test something without relying on the real part.
RSA: Rivest–Shamir–Adleman: a way to scramble information so it can be unlocked only with a matching secret key.
CADO-NFS: A program that helps break very large numbers into the smaller numbers that multiply to make them, using a specialized method.
GNFS: General Number Field Sieve: a method for finding the prime-number building blocks of a very large number.
cold reading: A way of seeming to know personal facts by making broad guesses, watching reactions, and adjusting what you say.
subjective validation: The tendency to think a vague statement is specifically true of you because it feels personally meaningful.
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a way to train an AI by having people rate its answers.
Forer effect: The tendency to see a general description as uniquely accurate about you, even though it could fit many people.
EEPROM: Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory: a chip that keeps data when power is off and can be rewritten with electricity.
RMA: Return Merchandise Authorization: approval and instructions for sending a product back for repair, replacement, or refund.
SKU: Stock Keeping Unit: a code a store uses to tell one product or version apart from others.
NDT test: Network Diagnostic Tool: a check of how quickly and reliably an internet connection can move data.
OSI model: Open Systems Interconnection model: a seven-layer map people use to explain how information moves between devices over a network.
local inference: Running an AI model on your own device instead of sending requests to a remote computer.
gravity: A setting in Hacker News's ranking formula that controls how quickly older posts lose position.
voting ring: A group of accounts that agree to upvote one another's submissions to push them higher in the rankings.
variable aperture: A camera lens opening whose size can change, letting in more or less light and affecting how much of the scene looks sharp.
bokeh: The soft, blurry look of out-of-focus parts of a photo, especially lights in the background.
pull request: A proposal to add your code changes to a shared project, usually asking others to review them first.
LaTeX: A system for writing and formatting documents, especially ones with equations, by marking how the text should appear.
token prefill: The step where an AI reads the supplied text before it starts writing an answer.
unified memory: A shared pool of working memory that a computer's main processor and graphics processor can both use, instead of each having a separate pool.
token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
embedding: A set of numbers that gives an AI a way to represent a word or piece of text and how it relates to others.
self-attention: A way for an AI to work out which other parts of the text matter most to each part it is reading.
air traffic control (ATC): Air traffic control: the people and systems that guide aircraft so they can travel safely without getting too close to one another.
failover: A backup system taking over automatically when the main one stops working.
steganography: Hiding a message inside an ordinary-looking file, such as a photo, so people do not notice it is there.
EXIF: Exchangeable Image File Format: information saved inside a photo file, such as when and where the photo was taken.
frequency domain: A way to describe an image or sound by its repeating patterns rather than by the position of each dot or moment.
CI: Continuous integration: automatic checks that run when developers change code, helping catch problems early.
runner: A computer or program that carries out an automated job, such as checking code.
sharding: Splitting data or work into separate parts so several computers can handle it more easily.
phoning home: When a program contacts its maker or another computer over the internet, often to report information or check for updates.
Asahi Linux: A project that makes the Linux operating system work on Macs with Apple-designed chips.
Pyodide: A project that lets Python code run inside a web browser without separately installing Python.
WSGI/ASGI: Web Server Gateway Interface / Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface: two standard ways for Python web apps to receive requests from a web server.
cold start: The extra wait while a service starts up after sitting unused.
vibe coding: Making software by telling an AI what you want and letting it write the code, often without closely checking how it works.
reward signal: Feedback that tells an AI during training whether an answer or action was good or bad.
code smell: A sign that code may have a deeper problem, even if it still works for now.
beam search: A way for an AI to keep several promising ways of continuing a sentence in mind, then choose among them.
DEFLATE: A method for shrinking files by replacing repeated patterns with shorter descriptions.
sliding window: A moving section of recent data that a program checks for patterns or repeats.
notification badge: A small dot or number on an app icon that shows there may be something new to check.
crib: A piece of a message that is known or guessed in advance and used to help decode the rest.
Bombe: A machine built during World War II to help find the settings used to encrypt German messages with Enigma.
cache reads: Using input that has been saved from an earlier request, rather than processing that same input from scratch again.
prompt injection: Instructions hidden in text or a file that try to trick an AI into ignoring its intended directions.
agentic coding: Having an AI handle coding tasks by making changes and checking its work with less step-by-step direction.
context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
grunt model: A less capable, cheaper AI model used for routine tasks so a stronger model can focus on harder ones.
bubblewrap: A tool that runs a program in a restricted space so it cannot freely access the rest of the computer.
systemd-nspawn: A Linux tool for starting a separate, contained Linux environment on the same computer.
rdrand: Read Random: a processor instruction that asks the chip to provide a random number.
microcode: Very low-level instructions inside a processor that help it carry out its operations.
CSPRNG: Cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator: a system that makes random-looking numbers that are extremely hard to guess.
Maven: A Palantir system used by the military to bring battlefield information together and help plan operations.
Palantir: A company that sells software for bringing together and analyzing information, including for governments and militaries.
logits: Scores an AI gives possible next words before choosing which one to use.
classifier: A program that sorts something into a category, such as deciding whether a message is spam.
moat: An advantage that makes it hard for competitors to take customers away from a business.
0-day: A software weakness its maker has not had time to fix yet, which attackers may use before a fix is ready.
PeopleSoft: Business software companies use to manage things like employee records, pay, and finances.
GrapheneOS: A privacy-focused version of Android, the software that runs many phones.
BYOD: Bring Your Own Device: a workplace policy that lets people use their personal phones or computers for work.
tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
DBC: Database Container: a FoxPro file that keeps the setup details for a group of related data files.
DBF: Database File: a file that stores a table of information, such as a list of names and details.
.fll: FoxPro Link Library: an add-on file that gives a FoxPro program extra functions.
SAML: Security Assertion Markup Language: a standard that lets one website tell another that you have signed in.
OIDC: OpenID Connect: a standard that lets you sign in to one service using an account from another.
canonicalization: Turning information into one agreed-upon form so computers can compare or check it consistently.
proof of concept: A small test or demo that shows whether an idea can work.
photovoltaics: The process of turning sunlight directly into electricity, as solar panels do.
GGUF: GPT-Generated Unified Format: a file type for saving an AI model so compatible programs can use it.
feature flag: A switch developers can use to turn a feature on or off without removing it from the program.
telemetry: Information a program sends back about how it is being used or whether it is working properly.
churn: The rate at which customers stop using a service or cancel it.
linter: A program that checks code for likely mistakes or inconsistent formatting.
private equity: Investment firms that buy whole companies, try to make them earn more, then sell them.
key performance indicators: Numbers or other measures a business watches to see whether it is meeting its main goals.
MAO inhibitors: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors: substances that slow the breakdown of certain brain chemicals; some medicines and tobacco smoke contain them.
cytisine: A medicine made from a plant that can reduce nicotine cravings and help people stop smoking.
harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
async tool calls: Requests to a tool that can finish later, letting a program do other work while it waits.
path traversal: A trick that uses a specially written file path to reach files a program was meant to keep off-limits.
RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
last mile: The short trip between a transit stop and where someone is actually going, often by walking, biking, or taking another ride.
tap-to-pay: Paying by briefly holding a bank card or phone near a payment reader.
POC: Proof of Concept: a small test or demo that checks whether an idea can work.
Resizable BAR: Resizable Base Address Register: a feature that lets a computer's main processor access more of a graphics card's memory at once, which can improve speed in some games.
UEFI: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface: the built-in startup software that checks a computer and starts its main software.
SMR: Small modular reactor: A nuclear power plant designed to be smaller and built in modules.
NIMBY: Not In My Back Yard: a phrase for people opposing a project near where they live.
decommission: To take a power plant out of service and deal with it when it is no longer operating.
kWh: Kilowatt-hour: a way to measure how much electricity is produced or used.
fission: The process of splitting atoms to release energy, which nuclear power plants use to make heat.
FOSS: Free and Open Source Software: apps whose code people can inspect, share, and change.
pre-approval API: A way for an app to ask Android to approve an install before the download finishes.
Kotlin: A programming language used to build Android apps.
Jetpack Compose: A toolkit developers use to build the screens of Android apps.
CJK: Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, grouped together here because their writing systems need special search support.
CRISPR: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats: a name for DNA patterns first noticed in bacteria, now used in tools for editing genes.
enzyme: A protein that helps chemical reactions happen in living things.
reverse transcriptase (RT): An enzyme that copies RNA into DNA.
DNA-repeat array: A long stretch of DNA with repeated sequences spaced along it.
ART: Array-associated reverse transcriptases: Anthropic’s name for the system of an enzyme, a nearby gene, and repeated DNA.
AI: Artificial intelligence: computer systems designed to do tasks people associate with thinking.
Streisand effect: When trying to hide something draws more attention to it instead.
upstreaming: Sending code changes to the main Linux project so they can become part of Linux itself.
device tree: A file that describes a device’s hardware so Linux knows how to work with it.
NPU: Neural Processing Unit: a chip part made to handle the kinds of calculations used by AI.
GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
OEM: Original Equipment Manufacturer: the company responsible for a laptop’s design and how its parts work together.
pawl: A little catch that can hold a gear in place; lifting it lets the gear move.
microcontroller: A tiny computer inside a device that tells the device what to do.
relay: A switch that a small electrical signal can turn on or off.
counterweight: A weight placed to balance another part, such as a clock hand.
lead-acid battery: A rechargeable battery that uses lead and acid to store power.
AR: Augmented reality: digital images or information added to what you see around you.
VR: Virtual reality: a computer-made view that replaces what you see around you.
Micro-OLED: A very small screen type that can show images inside a headset.
FOV: Field of view: how wide an area you can see through the glasses at once.
PPD: Pixels per degree: a measure of how much detail the display shows across your view.
6DoF: Six degrees of freedom: tracking that follows your position and which way you're facing.
passthrough: A headset view that uses cameras to show you the room around you.
SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
puck: A small separate box; here, it has a slot for expandable storage.
latency: The time between doing something and seeing the device respond.
postmortem: A review after an incident that looks at what happened and what should change.
signal-to-noise ratio: A way to describe how much useful information alerts provide compared with distracting alerts.
root cause: The one main reason people identify for a problem, though complex failures can have several causes.
5 whys: A way to investigate a problem by repeatedly asking why it happened.
regression test: A check to catch whether a change has brought back an old problem.
x-height: The height of lowercase letters that do not stick up or hang below the line.
baseline: The invisible line that most letters in a line of text sit on.
ligature: A special shape a font uses for a set of letters, sometimes replacing them with one different shape.
@font-face: A webpage instruction that tells a browser which font file to use.
unicode-range: A setting that says which letters and symbols a font should apply to.
surveillance pricing: Charging different people different prices based on information gathered about them.
data broker: A company that gathers information about people and sells or shares it.
algorithmic pricing: Using a computer program to set or test prices.
UX: User experience: how using a product feels and how easy it is to get things done.
WIMP: Windows, icons, menus, pointer: the familiar desktop setup where you use windows and menus with a pointer.
working memory: A desktop's ability to keep track of what you copied or gathered, so you can return to it later.
virtual desktop: A separate on-screen workspace where you can keep a different set of open windows.
tiling window manager: A desktop setup that arranges open windows in blocks instead of letting them overlap freely.
foreign agent: Someone acting for another country's government or promoting its goals.
FARA: Foreign Agents Registration Act: a US law that requires people acting for foreign governments to tell the government about that relationship.
CCP: Chinese Communist Party: China's ruling political party.
counterintelligence: Work by a government to find and stop spying or influence efforts by other countries.
data center: A building full of computers that store information and run online services.
ADP: Advanced Data Protection: Apple's optional iCloud setting that protects more kinds of data so Apple doesn't have what it needs to unlock them.
E2EE: End-to-end encryption: a way to protect data so only the people it's meant for can read it, not the company carrying it.
TCN: Technical Capability Notice: a UK legal order that can require a tech company to build or keep a way to meet certain requirements; it doesn't itself grant access to anyone's data.
backdoor: A way into a protected device or service that bypasses its normal security.
inference engine: Software that runs a trained AI model on input so it can produce a result.
open-weight model: A model whose trained settings are shared so other people can use them.
Pareto frontier: A set of choices where you can't get better on one measure without giving something up on another.
Jevons Paradox: The idea that when something gets more efficient, people may use more of it overall.
super PAC: A group that raises and spends money to support or oppose candidates, outside the candidates’ own campaigns.
wage theft: When a company fails to pay workers all the money they earned.
restitution: Money paid back to people who were wronged.
TTS: Text-to-speech: software that turns written words into spoken audio.
SynthID: Google’s built-in marker for generated audio, which helps people detect that it was made by AI.
C2PA credentials: Details attached to media that help show where it came from.
backchanneling: Short sounds like “mhm” or “yeah” that make it clear someone is listening.
flagging: Marking a post or comment for review; on Hacker News, enough flags can hide it from normal view.
karma: A user's standing on Hacker News; reaching a certain amount lets them flag posts.
burying: Moving a post lower in the rankings so fewer people see it.
frontier model: One of the most capable, newest AI models available.
benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
actuator: A part that turns a command into movement, such as steering or braking.
DNF: A label meaning the run did not finish.
MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
scholarly communication: The ways researchers share and discuss their work.
nonprofit: An organization that uses its money for its work instead of paying profits to owners.
LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
web of trust: A way to decide who to trust online by relying on people or groups you already trust.
PGP: Pretty Good Privacy: a tool for protecting messages and checking that they came from the person who sent them.
SSH: Secure Shell: a way to connect to another computer and send it commands over a network.
WebSockets: A way for two programs to keep a connection open and send messages back and forth.
PTY: Pseudo-terminal: a command window that a program can use as if someone had opened one.
Bash: A command-line shell that lets people run commands by typing them.
Tramp: An Emacs feature for working with files and commands on another computer.
Node: Software that lets JavaScript run outside a web browser.
applicant tracking system: Software employers use to collect and manage job applications.
median: The middle value when the results are put in order.
ghost job: A job ad that stays up even though the employer may not be actively hiring for it.
evergreen role: A role an employer keeps hiring for, so its job ad may stay up for a long time.
firmware update: A change to the built-in software that tells a device how to work.
IoT: Internet of Things: everyday devices connected to the internet so they can share information or be controlled remotely.
API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
AI agent: An autonomous computer program that can carry out tasks.
alignment: The effort to keep an AI's actions in line with what people want.
guardrails: Instructions that tell an AI how it should respond.
red teaming: Trying to find ways people could make an AI ignore its safety instructions.
bulk billing: A payment setup where a doctor bills Medicare directly for a visit instead of charging the patient.
anti-scraping measures: Website defenses meant to stop automated programs from collecting lots of its pages or data.
XSS: Cross-site scripting: A flaw that can make a website run instructions supplied by someone visiting it.
motherboard: The main circuit board inside a device, where many of its parts connect.
failsafe mode: A backup way for a device to keep doing its basic job when something goes wrong.
subnet router: A device that connects Tailscale users to devices on a local network.
app connector: A device that routes Tailscale traffic to an application that isn't running on a Tailscale device.
multi-queue: Several packet waiting lines that can be worked on at the same time.
tailnet: The private network of devices connected through Tailscale.
control plane: Tailscale's service that gives a device its map of other devices it can reach.
data plane: The part that carries the actual traffic between devices.
netmap caching: Saving a copy of the device map so a device can start connecting before it reaches Tailscale's control service.
WireGuard: A tool for making encrypted connections between devices.
userspace: The part of a computer where ordinary apps run, rather than the operating system's core.
kernel mode: Running code inside the core part of the operating system.
DERP: A Tailscale relay that helps pass traffic when two devices can't connect directly.
DPDK: A tool developers use to handle network traffic quickly outside the operating system's usual networking path.
SQL injection: A trick that smuggles commands into a website request to try to reveal or change saved information.
cross-site scripting: A trick that gets a website to run code supplied by someone visiting it.
agent swarm: A group of software agents working on tasks together.
malware: Software made to harm a computer or get access to it without permission.
.dmg: A Mac file that can be opened to access or install software.
DMCA takedown notice: Digital Millennium Copyright Act: a notice asking a website to remove material that someone says copies their work.
75th percentile: A point where three out of four measured results were at or below that time.
Mini-ITX: A small motherboard size used to fit computers into compact cases.
Wonderboard: A plastic sheet material the builder cut to make the computer's inner support case.
ducting: A passage that guides air where it needs to go.
dual boot: Setting up a computer so it can start in either of two operating systems.
public comment: A part of a meeting where members of the public can speak to local officials.
resolution: A formal proposal that a council can discuss and vote on.
B2B: Business-to-business: selling products or services to other companies, rather than individual people.
creator economy: The business around people who make online content and earn money from it.
MMU: Memory Management Unit: hardware that helps an operating system manage memory and keep programs separate.
SBC: Single-board computer: a whole small computer built onto one board.
PSRAM: Pseudo-static random-access memory: extra working space for a device's programs and data.
BSP: Board Support Package: software files that help an operating system work with a particular board.
XIP: Execute-in-place: running a program straight from storage, without first copying it into working memory.
OTG: On-The-Go: a USB mode that lets a device take charge of a connection to things like a keyboard.
mood boards: A set of pictures and ideas collected to show the look or feel someone wants for a design.
renders: Images made to show how a design might look.
OS: Operating system: the main software that runs a device and lets its apps work.
UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
lobe: One of the larger sections that make up an organ such as the liver.
primary sclerosing cholangitis: A long-term illness that damages the small tubes carrying bile through the liver.
immunosuppressants: Medicines that quiet the immune system so it is less likely to attack or reject something.
necrosis: When body tissue dies, often because it has been badly damaged or lost its blood supply.
teleology: Explaining a feature of nature as if it exists for a purpose, rather than asking how it came about.
agentic development: Using AI agents to carry out parts of building software.
backend: The part of an app that does work behind the scenes, such as handling its data.
framework: A collection of ready-made parts and rules that helps people build software.

non_exhaustive: A marker that tells code using a public type that more cases or fields may be added later.
muscle memory: A familiar action becoming automatic after you repeat it many times.

syscall: A request a program sends to the operating system to do something on its behalf.

geocoded pages: Pages linked to a place on a map, so a nearby search can find them.
wrapper: A small tool that gives an existing tool a different, often easier, way for people to use it.
natural language programming: Giving a computer instructions in everyday speech instead of a programming language.

specification: A written description of what a program should do.

bench: A test people use to compare how well different models handle a task.

consumer cooperative: A business owned by its customers, who get a say in how it is run.

UART: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter: a simple connection for sending data to and from a device’s electronics.
JTAG: Joint Test Action Group: a connection used to inspect or control chips inside a device.

security clearance: Permission to see government information that is kept secret.
digital sovereignty: A country’s ability to control the technology it relies on instead of depending on outside providers.
Starshield: The article’s name for the military version of Starlink.

acrostic: A message formed from the first letters of a series of words or lines.

functional programming: A way of writing code by combining functions while trying to avoid hidden changes to shared data.
bounds checks: Checks that make sure a program only reads or writes within a collection's valid range.
automatic reference counting: A system that tracks when a value is still being used and frees its memory when it is not.
pure function: A function that returns an answer without changing anything outside itself.
opportunistic mutation: Changing a value in place when nothing else is sharing it, instead of making a new copy.
copy elision: Skipping a copy so code can use the original value instead.

many-worlds interpretation: An interpretation where different possible outcomes all happen in separate branches of reality.

wave function collapse: The idea that a measurement turns a set of possible results into the one observed result.
instrumentalism: The view that a scientific theory is a useful tool for making predictions, not necessarily a literal description of reality.
falsifiable: A claim is falsifiable if an observation or experiment could show it is wrong.

cache: A place a program keeps data so it can reuse it instead of doing the work again.
dictionary compression: A way to shrink repeated data by storing distinct values once and referring to them.
DTLS 1.3: Datagram Transport Layer Security: a way to protect data sent over connections that can lose or reorder messages.

interop: When code in one language can use code written in another.

overload resolution: How C++ picks which version of a function to use when several share a name.
marshalling: Changing data into a form that lets different languages pass it back and forth.
ADL: Argument-dependent lookup: a C++ rule that helps find a function based on the kinds of values passed to it.

tapering off: Cutting down a medicine gradually rather than stopping all at once.
memory safety: Rules that stop a program from reading or changing the wrong parts of a computer’s working memory.

binding: A connector that lets one programming language use code written for another.
antimatter: Matter’s counterpart, which tends to destroy itself and ordinary matter when they meet.
positron: The antimatter counterpart of an electron.
quantum states: The different conditions a tiny particle can be in.
magnetic moment: A measure of the strength and direction of a particle’s magnetic field.

counter: A number a generator updates to distinguish IDs made around the same time.

universal high income: A hoped-for future where everyone has a high income.

Will: Schopenhauer’s name for the underlying reality he thought everything expresses; the essay says music represents it directly.

injection locking: When one repeating signal nudges another into matching its timing.
